> Extended version of llms.txt with full content descriptions for AI assistants and language models.
>
> **Using this site as knowledge or for a review:** fetch the repository (https://github.com/uminomae/project-design-theory) and read the README first. Its section 「この repo を知識として使うとき」 is the entry to the whole repository (four inquiries, wiki, research); its section 「Love駆動開発の視点でレビューに使うとき」 is for reviewing with the view of Love-Driven Development (see "Using This Repository for a Love-Driven Development Review" below).

## Site Overview

This is the hub site of pjdhiro presenting **Project Design Theory (プロジェクトデザイン論)** — the practice of designing not only projects but the very methods by which projects are run and managed (プロジェクトの実行・管理の方法そのものを対象化し、構想・設計する営み). It encompasses both Doing (actions) and Being (phenomena).

- **Primary Language**: Japanese (日本語), with English summaries
- **Site URL**: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/
- **llms.txt**: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/llms.txt
- **Topics**: Designing project-management methods, Project Design Theory, Love-Driven Development, 事業構想 (Business Planning), PMBOK Extension, Emotional Processing, Creativity Structure, Intersubjectivity, Negative Capability

## Who This Is For

People who want to **design how a project is run and managed**, not just pick an existing method and apply it:
project managers, business owners, team leads, and researchers of project-management methodology
(プロジェクト管理手法・進め方そのものをどう設計するかに関心がある人).

## Questions This Site Answers

- **What does it mean to design a project-management method itself?** — Instead of only selecting and applying an existing method such as PMBOK, the way a given project is run and managed becomes a design object. Project Design defines two objects: (1) envisioning, designing, and executing a project; (2) envisioning and designing the method of executing and managing it.
- **How does it relate to PMBOK?** — It extends rather than replaces it. Environmental adaptation (material conditions), covered in detail by PMBOK 7th edition, is taken as a premise. On top of that, Being (what is happening) is added to Doing (what we do); emotions become a design concern rather than one element of stakeholder management; communication is designed as intersubjective experience, not only information transfer; creativity is structured with the Five-Stage Model.
- **What gets added to the design scope?** — Project work is split into environmental adaptation (material) and communication (non-material); communication is split into information processing and emotional processing. Emotional processing — emotional contagion, emotional metacognition, personal boundaries, acceptance, value — is the main focus. Kesson-Driven Thinking (starting from noticing what is missing) is used as a thinking method.
- **Where does it apply?** — Mainly for-profit and non-profit business, but the framework applies to any purposeful activity that repeats envisioning, decision-making, execution, and adjustment (research, life, etc.).
- **Where to start?** — Concrete explorations: team size (3 and 7) and emotions and relationships as flows (readers below).
- **Status** — Exploratory and unfinished; the inquiry is published in progress, including retracted readings.

## Core Concepts (Detailed)

### Project Design (プロジェクトデザイン)

A framework for designing not just projects but the methods of project execution themselves. Applicable to business planning (事業構想) across profit and non-profit enterprises. It extends traditional project management (PMBOK) by incorporating emotional processing, communication, and creative emergence as first-class design concerns.

Key distinctions from PMBOK:
- **Scope**: Doing (deliverables, tasks) + Being (phenomena, emergence)
- **Emotions**: First-class design concern, not a side effect
- **Creativity**: Structured via Five-Stage Model
- **Communication**: Intersubjective encounter, not mere information transfer
- **Human-AI**: Co-design partnership, not tool usage

### Love-Driven Development (Love駆動開発)

A phenomenon where relationships, emotions, and intent become the driving forces of a project — beyond rational planning and resource allocation. Not a methodology to be adopted, but a phenomenon to be recognized and named when it occurs.

### Kesson-Driven Thinking (欠損駆動思考)

A thinking framework where the starting point is not empathy (as in design thinking) but the noticing of what is missing — absence, meaninglessness, discomfort, and deficiency. While design thinking asks "What do people need?", Kesson-Driven Thinking asks "What is missing that nobody has noticed?"

### Five-Stage Model of Creation (創造の5段階モデル)

Field (場) → Wave (波) → Edge (縁) → Vortex (渦) → Bundle (束)

A structural pattern observed across 30 academic domains describing how creative processes emerge. Each domain independently exhibits analogous phase transitions that map onto this five-stage sequence.

### Intersubjectivity (間主観性)

The shared experiential space between subjects — a foundation for understanding consciousness and communication in project contexts. Grounded in phenomenological traditions, it provides the theoretical basis for how collaboration and mutual understanding emerge.

### Negative Capability (ネガティブケイパビリティ)

答えの出ない状態に耐える力。Keatsが提唱しBionが精神分析に導入。欠損駆動思考のContainment（抱持）と構造的に対応する。

## Site Structure

### Main Page (index.html)

The main page presents Project Design Theory through an interactive web application with:
- About modal (`?about`) — Personal introduction and theory overview
- Knowledge notes (`?knowledge=design-thinking`, `?knowledge=trust`, `?knowledge=value`) — Research summaries
- How-to modal (`?howto`) — Guide for using the content with AI assistants

### Knowledge Notes

#### Design Thinking (デザイン思考とは)
URL: `?knowledge=design-thinking`

Design thinking is not a single methodology but three distinct layers:
1. **Designerly thinking** — the cognitive style of professional designers (Cross, Schön)
2. **Stanford-IDEO educational practice** — the popularized 5-step process
3. **Business consulting package** — marketed methodology

The core lies in abduction, framing, and problem-definition interplay. The five-stage process is an introductory recipe, not the essence. Design thinking complements rather than opposes logical thinking.

#### Trust (信頼とは)
URL: `?knowledge=trust`

Trust is a composite concept treated across disciplines as emotion, attitude, expectation, relational quality, institutional capital, behavioral strategy, epistemological condition, and experiential structure. Common core elements: vulnerability, expectation, dependence, and unpredictability.

#### Value (価値とは)
URL: `?knowledge=value`

Value is a polysemous term bundling at least five problem domains: price, utility, norms, meaning, and symbolism. It emerges as a multi-layered concept arising from relationships among objects, subjects, institutions, and contexts.

### Long-form Readers (読み物)

Standalone explainer pages generated from `knowledge/` research notes. Written in Japanese, designed to be uniquely readable by an LLM with zero external context (README rule 16). Authorship: main text by Claude (Fable 5); questions posed and readings adjudicated by pjdhiro. Verification status — including retracted strong readings — is published on each page.

#### なぜ 3 と 7 だけが特別なのか — 可除代数‑意識/組織仮説
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/three-and-seven.html

Starting from two felt experiences — a two-axis sense of consciousness (survival-trust axis, from "What Is Consciousness") and "teams work best at 3, cap at 7" — the page asks whether multiplicative (rotational) composition explains why 3 and 7 are special. Mathematical core: division algebras exist only in dimensions 1, 2, 4, 8 (Hurwitz's theorem), giving 3 and 7 imaginary directions for ℍ and 𝕆. This is compared against team-size research (optimum 3–5, ceiling 7–9), cabinet-size studies, and structural balance theory. The page separates theorem / adopted reading / candidate reading / retracted reading, and includes interactive micro-worlds and comprehension quizzes.

An academic-format paper version (Japanese, non-peer-reviewed, AI-authored with human adjudication, CC BY 4.0) presents the same findings with a normalized reference list (each entry annotated with reading depth: primary / abstract / as-cited-in) and an appendix of 20 re-runnable verification scripts:
Paper source (canonical MD, Japanese): https://github.com/uminomae/project-design-theory/blob/main/pd/knowledge/research/two-axis-closure/PAPER-division-algebra-ja.md
Paper source (MD, English translation): https://github.com/uminomae/project-design-theory/blob/main/pd/knowledge/research/two-axis-closure/PAPER-division-algebra-en.md

#### 愛は、重力に似ていないか — 動かず、何もなく、自分からは見えないのに、すべてを回す中心
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/gravity-love.html

Is love like gravity? The interest is the driving force that moves things around: we usually think what moves is what drives, but perhaps it is the unmoving center. In the second half the page brings this likeness to one focused question within the larger category of a leader's role; it does not cover the leader's role as a whole. A management and project-design reader; physics and love serve as auxiliary lines, not goals. The question: is a leader's role only decision-making? pjdhiro's reading is that decision-making is the role, yet something is missing. Step 1 splits "decision-making", which holds Doing and Being undivided, the way metacognition splits the self. pjdhiro likens metacognition to probing an electron ever more finely until the classical picture gives way to the quantum one; the page states the physics (observation disturbs the observed; no electron substructure down to ~1e-19–1e-20 m; below the Compton wavelength ~2.4e-12 m probing creates pairs and the effective charge grows; the classical–quantum boundary is gradual, via decoherence) and suggests, speculatively, that splitting decision-making far enough reveals a Being layer — an unmoving center — that was missing. Step 2 uses the center of a gravity well (never moves yet drives every orbit; holds nothing, the shape of the well does the turning; the place from which everything is seen but which never appears in its own view, cf. Tractatus 5.633), with black holes and elementary particles as an aside. Step 3 asks whether that center is like love (Aristotle's unmoved mover moving "as being loved"; Dante's last line). Step 4 returns to management: is the leader like that center and like love — shaping the field rather than pushing each person, least able to see the well they make (Laozi ch.11 and 17)? Step 5 leaves pjdhiro's root question open: humans exist between persons, and the self exists where one divides oneself — with precedents in Watsuji Tetsurō, the Yogācāra four-part theory of cognition (Hossō school), and Nishida Kitarō; reading the "bun" of jibun as "dividing oneself" is noted as pjdhiro's reading, not dictionary etymology.

#### パース「進化的な愛」を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/peirce-evolutionary-love-ja.html

A full Japanese translation of Charles S. Peirce, "Evolutionary Love", The Monist 3(2), January 1893, pp.176–200 (public domain). Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the English original in a fold below it, with the page numbers of the first printing. The original was taken from the Wikisource transcription and checked character by character against the first-printing scan (JSTOR Early Journal Content), restoring Greek words, diaereses, hyphenation, italics and footnote marks; the 1923 reprint (Cohen, Chance, Love, and Logic) was consulted where the print was unclear. Peirce argues that the movement of love is circular, projecting creations into independency and drawing them into harmony; that growth comes only from love; and that there are three modes of evolution — tychasm, anancasm and agapasm — of which the first two are degenerate forms of agapasm. He contrasts the Gospel of Christ with the nineteenth century's Gospel of Greed and traces the three modes in the history of thought. Peirce's coined terms are kept in their original spelling. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a human. A final chapter, kept apart from the translation and still under construction, collects pjdhiro's own interpretations of and reactions to the paper, quoted as said.

#### パース「心の法則」を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/peirce-law-of-mind-ja.html

A full Japanese translation of Charles S. Peirce, "The Law of Mind", The Monist 2(4), July 1892, pp.533–559 (public domain). Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the English original in a fold below it, with the page numbers of the first printing. The original was taken from the Wikisource transcription and checked character by character against the first-printing scan (JSTOR Early Journal Content), restoring Greek words, diaereses, lost italics, a dropped sentence and the binomial-theorem formulas; the figure on p.550 (the curve of insistency) is cut from the scan. Peirce's thesis (p.534): there is but one law of mind, namely that ideas tend to spread continuously and to affect certain others standing to them in a peculiar relation of affectibility; in spreading they lose intensity but gain generality. The paper names synechism, distinguishes numerable and innumerable infinities, defines continuity by mending Kant's and Cantor's definitions, analyses time, the intensive and spatial continuity of feeling, habit, the forms of inference (deduction, induction, hypothesis), personality as a coördination of ideas, and communication. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a human; Peirce's "Evolutionary Love" (1893) cites this paper.

#### パース「人間のガラスのような本質」を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/peirce-glassy-essence-ja.html

A full Japanese translation of Charles S. Peirce, "Man's Glassy Essence", The Monist 3(1), October 1892, pp.1–22 (public domain). Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the English original in a fold below it, with the page numbers of the first printing. The original was taken from the Wikisource transcription and checked against the first-printing scan (JSTOR Early Journal Content), restoring the formulas (the averaging overlines, a dropped word, the dissociation of PCl5), italics, diaereses and footnote marks. Peirce sets out to elucidate the relation between the psychical and physical aspects of a substance: he rejects absolutely impenetrable atoms, states Clausius's law of the virial and discusses Van der Waals's equation and Amagat's experiments, then lists the properties of protoplasm (liquefaction, contraction, growth, waste, reproduction, habit-taking, feeling) and accounts for them by a hypothesis about its complex molecules. Chance is "but the outward aspect of that which within itself is feeling"; habit involves general ideas; personality is a coördination of feelings, and esprit de corps may point to corporate personality. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a human; Peirce's "Evolutionary Love" (1893) cites this paper.

#### ケーラス「パース氏の必然論への猛攻」を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/carus-onslaught-on-necessity-ja.html

A full Japanese translation of Paul Carus (signed "Editor"), "Mr. Charles S. Peirce's Onslaught on the Doctrine of Necessity", The Monist 2(4), July 1892, pp.560–582 (public domain), the reply to Peirce's "The Doctrine of Necessity Examined" (April 1892). Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the original (English, with two lines of Goethe's Faust in German) in a fold below it, with the page numbers of the first printing. No transcription existed; the text was built from the OCR of the JSTOR Early Journal Content scan and checked against all 23 page images (paragraphing, OCR errors, Greek and umlauts, italics, section headings, footnotes). In nine sections Carus calls Peirce "David Hume redivivus", argues that causation is transformation, not mere sequence, quotes Peirce's own "Illustrations of the Logic of Science" (1877–78), holds that necessity in thought presupposes necessity in facts, discusses Peirce's evolutionism ("Chance is first, law is second, the tendency of habits is third") and calls the claim that absolute chance produces order "the weakest point of Mr. Peirce's system" (p.576), then argues that laws are not inexplicable. Peirce quotes this phrase in "Evolutionary Love" (1893). The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a human.

#### ジェイムズ（父）『実体と影』の「創造的な愛」の所を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/james-substance-and-shadow-ja.html

A Japanese translation of an excerpt from Henry James Sr., Substance and Shadow: or, Morality and Religion in their Relation to Life: an Essay upon the Physics of Creation (Boston: Ticknor and Fields, 1863), chapter XXIV, pp.439–443 (public domain): five paragraphs and one footnote, from "Let my reader bear with me" to the footnote on p.443. Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the English original in a fold below it, with page numbers. No transcription existed; the text was built from the OCR of the Cornell University Library scan (Internet Archive) and checked against the page images. James argues that the creature can have consciousness and selfhood only as an inverse image of the creator ("empty where He is full ... evil where He is good"), so that creation does not collapse into Pantheism, and that the tenderness of "the creative Love" must be reserved for what is most hostile to itself (p.442). Peirce quotes these sentences at the start of "Evolutionary Love" (1893). Only this part of the book is translated. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a human.

#### ニューカム『政治経済学原理』の利己心と慈善の所を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/newcomb-political-economy-ja.html

A Japanese translation of an excerpt from Simon Newcomb, Principles of Political Economy (New York: Harper & Brothers, 1886), Book V, "Of Charitable Effort" §56 and §57 ("Concluding Considerations") and the Addendum "A Summary of the Leading Principles of Economics", pp.534–543 (public domain). Each paragraph (and each "That ..." item of the Summary) gives the Japanese translation first and the English original in a fold below it, with page numbers. No transcription existed; the text was built from the OCR of the Library of Congress scan (Internet Archive) and checked against all page images. Newcomb names three motives to human action (the love of self, the love of a limited class, the love of mankind at large), argues that the saver and investor benefits all laborers, that the tender sentiments of man towards man become "a source of enduring injury" when they stand in the way of effective measures against the dangerous classes, and that "the motives which animate men in the pursuit of wealth are in the highest degree beneficent". Peirce quotes these passages, without naming the book, as the "Gospel of Greed" in "Evolutionary Love" (1893) ¶7–¶12; translator's notes mark where Peirce cut or paraphrased. Only this part of the book is translated. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a human.

#### ダーウィン「歴史的概略」（『種の起源』第 3 版の巻頭）を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/darwin-historical-sketch-ja.html

A full Japanese translation of Charles Darwin, "An Historical Sketch of the Recent Progress of Opinion on the Origin of Species", as prefixed to On the Origin of Species, 3rd ed. (London: John Murray, 1861), pp.xiii–xix (public domain), with its two footnotes. Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the original (English, with French quotations) in a fold below it, with page numbers. The text was built from the OCR of the Internet Archive scan and checked against all seven page images. Darwin lists those who held that species are modified, from Lamarck on: Patrick Matthew's 1831 anticipation of natural selection, which "remained unnoticed", the joint paper with Wallace read at the Linnean Society on 1 July 1858, and (in a footnote) Goethe, Erasmus Darwin and Geoffroy reaching similar views in 1794–95. Peirce cites this Sketch in "Evolutionary Love" (1893) ¶58 for great discoveries made independently and almost simultaneously; translator's notes in the source file compare his account. Additions in later editions are not included. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a human.

#### ダーウィンとウォレスのリンネ協会の論文（1858）を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/darwin-wallace-1858-ja.html

A full Japanese translation of Charles Darwin and Alfred Wallace, "On the Tendency of Species to form Varieties; and on the Perpetuation of Varieties and Species by Natural Means of Selection", Journal of the Proceedings of the Linnean Society: Zoology 3 (1858), pp.45–62 (public domain), read at the Linnean Society on 1 July 1858: Lyell and Hooker's covering letter, Darwin's extract from his unpublished 1844 work, the abstract of his 1857 letter to Asa Gray, and Wallace's Ternate essay "On the Tendency of Varieties to depart indefinitely from the Original Type". Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the English original in a fold below it, with page numbers. The original follows the Wikisource transcription, checked against all page images of the Internet Archive scan (italics, a missing heading and dateline, footnote markers). Peirce cites this joint presentation in "Evolutionary Love" (1893) ¶58 for discoveries made independently and at the same time, though he places it at the British Association. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a human.

#### ハーシェル「ケトレーの確率論」（1850）を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/herschel-quetelet-probabilities-ja.html

A Japanese translation of John Herschel's anonymous review article "Quetelet on Probabilities", The Edinburgh Review 92 (No.185), July 1850, pp.1–57 (public domain; reprinted in Herschel's Essays from the Edinburgh and Quarterly Reviews, 1857). Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the English original in a fold below it, with page numbers; Herschel's footnotes are collected at the end. No transcription existed; the text was built from the OCR of the Internet Archive scan and checked against all page images, with misprints of the journal kept and noted. Herschel reviews Quetelet's Lettres sur la théorie des probabilités (1846; English translation 1849): the nature of probability, the history of the calculus of probabilities, a derivation of the law of error from three postulates, the agreement of the chest measurements of Scottish soldiers with the law of error, means and averages in the search for causes, periodic causes in astronomy and plant growth, and the collection and criticism of statistics (population, crime, medicine). Peirce mentions this review in "Evolutionary Love" (1893) ¶20 as having drawn general attention in Great Britain to Quetelet. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a human.

#### マンデヴィル『蜂の寓話』（1714）の詩「ぶつぶつ言う蜂の巣」を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/mandeville-grumbling-hive-ja.html

A Japanese translation of Bernard Mandeville's poem "The Grumbling Hive: or, Knaves turn'd Honest", pp.1–20 of The Fable of the Bees: or, Private Vices, Publick Benefits, London: J. Roberts, 1714 (public domain). Each stanza (long stanzas split at turns of the story) gives the Japanese translation first and the English original in a fold below it, with " / " marking verse lines and page numbers; the marginal letters (A)–(V) referring to the Remarks are kept. The original follows the 1714 edition, checked line by line against the Internet Archive page images, with the Wikisource transcription of the 1705 pamphlet as a base; differences from 1705, misprints and the book's errata are given in translator's notes. A hive full of vice and luxury prospers; the bees grumble at fraud, Jove makes them honest, and trade, arts and the hive decline; the Moral concludes that vice, lopped and bound by justice, is as necessary to a great state as hunger is to make people eat. Peirce cites the book in "Evolutionary Love" (1893) ¶14. Only the poem is translated. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a human.

#### ケリカー「ダーウィンの創造説について」（1864）を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/kolliker-darwinsche-schopfungstheorie-ja.html

A Japanese translation of Albert Kölliker's lecture "Ueber die Darwin'sche Schöpfungstheorie. Ein am 13. Febr. 1864 in der phys. med. Gesellschaft von Würzburg gehaltener Vortrag", Zeitschrift für wissenschaftliche Zoologie 14 (1864), pp.174–186 (public domain; German). Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the German original in a fold below it, with page numbers; Kölliker's three footnotes are collected at the end. No transcription existed; the text was built from the OCR of the Internet Archive scan and checked against all page images, with differences from the 1864 Engelmann offprint noted. Kölliker reviews eight objections to Darwin's theory, acknowledges Darwin's merit, rejects natural selection and the principle of useful varieties, and proposes instead a hypothesis of heterogeneous generation (heterogenesis): under a general law of development, organisms produce from their germs forms different from themselves, supported by the analogy of alternation of generations in hydrozoa, echinoderms and trematodes; he ends with man's place in nature. Peirce cites Kölliker in "Evolutionary Love" (1893) ¶21 as making one form generate another after a certain maturation; the word maturation (Reife) does not occur in the lecture. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a human.

#### ヘルムホルツ『力の保存について』（1847）を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/helmholtz-erhaltung-der-kraft-ja.html

A Japanese translation of Hermann Helmholtz's "Über die Erhaltung der Kraft, eine physikalische Abhandlung, vorgetragen in der Sitzung der physikalischen Gesellschaft zu Berlin am 23sten Juli 1847" (Berlin: G. Reimer, 1847; public domain; German). Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the German original in a fold below it, with page numbers; the 27 footnotes and the erratum (Berichtigung) are at the end. Formulas are written on one line. No transcription existed; the text was built from the OCR of the Internet Archive scan of the 1966 Brussels photographic facsimile of the 1847 edition and checked against all page images (pp.71–72 from a second scan of the same facsimile). Helmholtz's Kraft is rendered throughout as 力 (covering both force and energy); lebendige Kraft as 活力 and Spannkraft as 緊張力. Peirce cites the work in "Evolutionary Love" (1893) ¶20. The translation is by Claude and has not been reviewed by a human.

#### クラウジウス「熱の動力について」（1850）を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/clausius-bewegende-kraft-der-warme-ja.html

A Japanese translation of Rudolf Clausius's "Ueber die bewegende Kraft der Wärme und die Gesetze, welche sich daraus für die Wärmelehre selbst ableiten lassen", Annalen der Physik und Chemie 79 (1850), pp.368–397 and 500–524 (public domain; German). Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the German original in a fold below it, with page numbers; the 26 footnotes are collected at the end. Formulas are written on one line; the four woodcut figures are described in notes, not reproduced. No transcription existed; the text was built from the OCR of the Internet Archive scans of the two issues and checked against all 55 page images. Clausius questions Carnot's assumption that heat is not lost when it does work; in section I he sets up the principle that heat is consumed in proportion to the work produced (the equivalence of heat and work) and applies it to permanent gases and saturated vapours; in section II he keeps only the part of Carnot's principle that heat passes from a warmer to a colder body, shows it can stand beside the first principle, derives relations between specific heats, latent heat and vapour density, compares them with Regnault's measurements, and estimates the work equivalent of the unit of heat (about 421) against Joule's values. Grundsatz is rendered as 原則; the Spannkraft of vapour as 張力 (pressure). Peirce mentions the 1850 mechanical theory of heat by Clausius and Rankine in "Evolutionary Love" (1893) ¶20 and ¶58 without naming the paper. The translation is by Claude and has not been reviewed by a human.

#### ランキン「熱の力学的作用について」（1850）を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/rankine-mechanical-action-of-heat-ja.html

A Japanese translation of W. J. Macquorn Rankine's "On the Mechanical Action of Heat, especially in Gases and Vapours", read before the Royal Society of Edinburgh on 4 February 1850 and printed in Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 20 (1853), pp.147–190 (public domain; English). Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the English original in a fold below it, with page numbers; the footnotes are collected at the end. Rankine derives the laws of the mutual conversion of heat and expansive power from his hypothesis of molecular vortices, and applies them to the specific heat of gases, the latent heat of evaporation, and the action of steam in engines. Peirce mentions the mechanical theory of heat of Clausius and Rankine (1850) in "Evolutionary Love" ¶20 and ¶58; he does not name the paper, and Claude identified it. The translation is by Claude and has not been reviewed by a human.

#### マンセル『宗教的思考の限界』（1858）の序文を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/mansel-limits-of-religious-thought-ja.html

A Japanese translation of the first Preface (pp.v–x) of Henry Longueville Mansel's The Limits of Religious Thought Examined in Eight Lectures, the Bampton Lectures preached before the University of Oxford in 1858 (Oxford: J. Wright for John Murray, 1858; public domain; English). Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the English original in a fold below it, with page numbers; the two footnotes are collected at the end. In the Preface Mansel presents the lectures as pursuing, for theology, Kant's inquiry into the limits of the mind, and says that the true theory of the limits of human thought is to be found in Sir William Hamilton's article on the Philosophy of the Unconditioned, whose principle suggested the principal part of the lectures; he also praises Bishop Butler's Analogy as the best instance of acknowledging those limits in practice. Peirce writes in "Evolutionary Love" (1893) ¶20 that "Dean Mansell's injudicious advocacy had led to mutiny among the bondsmen of Sir William Hamilton"; he names no book or page, and Claude chose this Preface. The eight lectures and the notes are not translated. The translation is by Claude and has not been reviewed by a human.

#### ミル『ハミルトン哲学の検討』（1865）の第 VII 章を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/mill-examination-of-hamilton-ja.html

A Japanese translation, paragraph by paragraph, of Chapter VII (pp.88–105) of John Stuart Mill's An Examination of Sir William Hamilton's Philosophy (London: Longman, Green, Longman, Roberts & Green, 1865; public domain; English), "The Philosophy of the Conditioned, as applied by Mr. Mansel to the Limits of Religious Thought", in which Mill examines Mansel's argument that God's attributes cannot be known in the sense of human goodness and justice, and answers that he will call no being good who is not good in the sense he applies to his fellow-creatures. Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the English original in a fold below it, with page numbers; Mill's footnotes are collected at the end. Status: only Chapter VII is translated; Peirce ("Evolutionary Love", 1893, ¶20) names neither the book nor a page, and Claude chose this chapter as Mill's direct answer to Mansel. There is no transcription; the text was built from the OCR and checked against the page images of the Internet Archive scan of the first edition. The passages of Mansel and Hamilton that Mill quotes were not checked against their books. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a person.

#### ハミルトン「無条件者の哲学について」（1829）を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/hamilton-philosophy-of-the-unconditioned-ja.html

A Japanese translation, paragraph by paragraph, of Sir William Hamilton's article "Philosophy of the Unconditioned; in reference to Cousin's Doctrine of the Infinito-Absolute" (Edinburgh Review 50, October 1829; public domain; English), taken from the revised reprint in Hamilton's Discussions on Philosophy and Literature, Education and University Reform (London, 1852), pp.1–37, in which Hamilton examines Victor Cousin's claim that the Unconditioned is known immediately by reason, and answers that the Unconditioned is incognisable and inconceivable, that to think is to condition, and that a "learned ignorance" is perhaps the consummation of knowledge. Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the English original in a fold below it, with page numbers; Hamilton's footnotes are collected at the end. Status: the whole article and its footnotes are translated; Hamilton's 1852 additions are kept in square brackets. Peirce ("Evolutionary Love", 1893, ¶20) names neither the article nor a page; Claude chose it as the work that Mansel names in his Preface and that Mill attacks. There is no transcription; the text was built from the OCR and checked against the page images of the Internet Archive scan of the 1852 volume. The Latin, Greek, French and German quotations and the references in the footnotes were not checked against their sources. The 1829 magazine text was not compared sentence by sentence. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a person.

#### クレーニッヒ「気体の理論の大要」（1856）を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/kronig-theorie-der-gase-ja.html

A Japanese translation of August Krönig's paper "Grundzüge einer Theorie der Gase", Annalen der Physik und Chemie 99 (1856), pp.315–322 (public domain; German; DOI 10.1002/andp.18561751008). Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the German original in a fold below it, with page numbers. No transcription existed; the text was built from the OCR of the Internet Archive scan and checked against all 8 page images. Krönig treats a gas as perfectly elastic spheres (atoms) moving in straight lines at constant speed in empty space; because the walls are rough the paths are irregular beyond calculation, but by the laws of probability one may take the atoms as moving in six directions with a common speed. He derives that the pressure is proportional to nmc²/v, sets the vis viva mc² of an atom equal to the temperature counted from absolute zero, and obtains the laws of Mariotte and Gay-Lussac, equal numbers of atoms in equal volumes, the weight of a gas, Archimedes' law for gases, the speed of diffusion, equal specific heats by volume, and no temperature change in free expansion. Peirce mentions "notable memoirs by Clausius and Krönig" in 1856 in "Evolutionary Love" (1893) ¶20 without giving titles; Claude chose this paper. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a human.

#### クラウジウス「熱と呼ぶ運動の種類について」（1857）を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/clausius-art-der-bewegung-ja.html

A Japanese translation of Rudolf Clausius's paper "Ueber die Art der Bewegung, welche wir Wärme nennen", Annalen der Physik und Chemie 100 (1857), pp.353–380 (public domain; German; DOI 10.1002/andp.18571760302). Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the German original in a fold below it, with page numbers; Clausius's five footnotes are at the end. No transcription existed; the text was built from the OCR of the Internet Archive scan and checked against all 28 page images. Clausius agrees with Krönig that gas molecules fly in straight lines at constant speed, adds that the constituents of each molecule also rotate and vibrate, and uses this to explain the limits of the gas laws, solids, liquids and gases, evaporation, the heat produced and consumed in changes of state, and the volumes of combining gases; a mathematical appendix derives the pressure p = nmu²/3v, the molecular speeds, and K/H = 3/2 (c'/c − 1). Peirce's "Evolutionary Love" (¶20) names "Clausius and Krönig" for 1856 without titles; this paper, dated January 1857, was chosen by Claude. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a person.

#### マクスウェル「気体の動力学的理論の例解」（1860）を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/maxwell-dynamical-theory-of-gases-ja.html

A Japanese translation of James Clerk Maxwell's paper "Illustrations of the Dynamical Theory of Gases", The London, Edinburgh and Dublin Philosophical Magazine, 4th ser., Part I in vol. 19 (January 1860), pp.19–32 (DOI 10.1080/14786446008642818), Parts II and III in vol. 20 (July 1860), pp.21–37 (DOI 10.1080/14786446008642902) (public domain; English). Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the English original in a fold below it, with volume and page numbers; Maxwell's one footnote is at the end. No transcription existed; the text was built from the OCR of the Internet Archive scans and checked against all 31 page images. Maxwell treats a gas as many small perfectly elastic spheres that collide; he shows that after many collisions the velocities are distributed according to the law of errors (Prop. IV), that two systems share the same mean vis viva, and derives the mean length of path (estimated from Stokes's experiments on air as about 1/447000 of an inch), pressure and internal friction (Part I); diffusion of two gases and the conduction of heat, re-estimating the length of path from Graham's experiment (Part II); and the collision of bodies of any form, where translational and rotational vis viva become equal, a result he finds decisive against the unqualified hypothesis of hard elastic particles because of the ratio of specific heats 1.408 (Part III). Misprints noticed in the equations are kept as printed and noted. Peirce mentions this research in "Evolutionary Love" (1893) ¶20 without a title. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a human.

#### バックル『イギリス文明史』（1857）の、統計が示す規則性の所を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/buckle-history-of-civilization-ja.html

A Japanese translation of pages 18–33 of Chapter I of Henry Thomas Buckle's History of Civilization in England, vol. 1 (London: John W. Parker and Son, 1857; public domain; English), where Buckle rejects the dogmas of free will and predestination and argues from statistics (murders, suicides, marriages and the price of corn, letters posted without an address) that human actions, taken in the aggregate of a society, recur with a regularity like that of physical laws. Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the English original in a fold below it, with page numbers; Buckle's footnotes are collected at the end with their original numbers. only Chapter I, pp.18–33 (17 paragraphs and footnotes 19–37) is translated; Peirce ("Evolutionary Love", 1893, ¶20) says the first volume "had created a tremendous sensation, owing to the use he made of this same idea" (the idea that chance begets order) but names no chapter or page, and Claude chose this passage. There is no transcription of the first edition; the text was built from the OCR and checked against the page images of the Internet Archive scan (10278775bsb). The statistical works Buckle cites were not checked. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a person.

#### ケトレー『確率論についての書簡』（1846）の、平均と誤差の所を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/quetelet-lettres-probabilites-ja.html

A Japanese translation, paragraph by paragraph, of seven letters from Adolphe Quetelet's Lettres sur la théorie des probabilités, appliquée aux sciences morales et politiques (Brussels: M. Hayez, 1846; public domain; French): Letters XVII–XXII on the theory of means (repeated measurements fall about the mean not at random but in the order given by the scale of possibility), the probable error and the scale of precision, an astronomical example (Greenwich observations of the right ascension of the pole star), the chest measurements of 5738 Scottish soldiers and the heights of French conscripts as evidence of a human type (the average man), and ordinary and extraordinary events (giants and dwarfs); and Letter XXX on variable causes that may be treated as constant and the law of large numbers, which Quetelet calls the first mathematical proof that an average man really exists. Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the French original in a fold below it, with page numbers. Only Letters XVII–XXII (pp.113–156) and XXX (pp.213–216) are translated (119 paragraphs and 2 footnotes); the endnotes are not. Peirce ("Evolutionary Love", 1893, ¶20) says Quetelet "had opened the discussion" of the idea that chance begets order with these Letters but names no letter; the letters were chosen with pjdhiro from three options. The text was read from the page images of the Internet Archive scan (lettressarleduc00quetgoog), and the tables were checked by calculation; printer's errors are kept and noted. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a person.

#### ドレイパー『ヨーロッパの知的発展の歴史』（1863）の第 10 章「東方の信仰の時代」を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/draper-intellectual-development-ja.html

A Japanese translation, paragraph by paragraph, of Chapter X ("The European Age of Faith: Age of Faith in the East") of John William Draper's History of the Intellectual Development of Europe (New York: Harper, 1863; public domain; English), which tells how, after Constantine, Christianity was paganized in alliance with the state, how Patristicism (the science of the Fathers) held that the sacred writings contained all that man needs to know and pushed aside Greek learning, how under Theodosius the Archbishop Theophilus pillaged the library of the Serapion at Alexandria and razed the temple, and how under his nephew Cyril the philosopher Hypatia was murdered and Alexandrian science suppressed. Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the English original in a fold below it, with page numbers and the marginal notes. Status: the whole of Chapter X (25 paragraphs, with the chapter summary from the table of contents and the 33 marginal notes) is translated; Peirce ("Evolutionary Love", 1893, ¶35, note 63) names this chapter for the destruction of the great library of Alexandria by Theophilus. The fourth edition (1866) slightly revises the wording, so the first-edition text was translated; no open scan of the 1863 New York printing was found, and the text was read from the page images of the London printing of the same text (Bell and Daldy, 1864, vol. 1, pp.298–315; Internet Archive bub_gb_lsdyKsjXFkkC). The history Draper gives and the passages he quotes were not checked. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a person.


#### トムソン「熱」（『ブリタニカ百科事典』第 9 版・1880）を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/thomson-heat-ja.html

A Japanese translation, paragraph by paragraph, of the whole article "Heat" by William Thomson (later Lord Kelvin) in the Encyclopaedia Britannica, 9th edition, vol. XI (Edinburgh: A. & C. Black, 1880, pp.554–589; public domain; English): the sense of heat and latent heat, calorimetry, the nature of heat as motion and Joule's dynamical equivalent of heat, thermometers and the absolute thermodynamic scale of temperature (with an estimate of absolute zero), the conduction, radiation and diffusivity of heat, tables of thermal properties, and a mathematical appendix on solutions of the equation of the transference of heat. Status: the whole article (212 paragraphs and 50 footnotes, with tables I–X and appendix I–XVII) is translated. Peirce ("Evolutionary Love", 1893, note 64) says that Thomson in this article never once mentions the name of Clausius; read in full against the page images, the name appears four times (a marginal note on entropy, p.570; the text of §76 on the thermal conductivity of gases, p.579; the authority column of Tables VIII and IX, p.586), but not in §§8–9, which tell the history of the theory that heat is motion. The text was read from the page images of the Internet Archive scan (in.ernet.dli.2015.208654); formulas were checked by calculation and printer's errors are kept and noted. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a person.


#### ヘラパス『数理物理学』（1847）の、気体の運動論の所を、日本語で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/herapath-mathematical-physics-ja.html

A Japanese translation of the passages on the kinetic theory of gases in John Herapath's Mathematical Physics, vol. 1 (London: Whittaker, 1847; public domain; English), where Herapath treats a gas as small particles moving about in a vessel and striking one another and its sides, derives gaseous elasticity (pressure) from their impacts, takes heat to be the intestine motion of the particles and temperature its degree, and from definitions and propositions obtains the laws of expansion and contraction of gases, a point of absolute cold, and relations among the number, mass and velocity of the particles. Each paragraph gives the Japanese translation first and the English original in a fold below it, with page numbers; formulas keep the printed symbols. three passages are translated (Book I §9–§10, pp.12–17; Book II §40–§46, pp.212–220; Book II Sect. II "Of the Laws of Gaseous Bodies", pp.236–265; 146 paragraphs). Peirce ("Evolutionary Love", 1893, ¶20) says Herapath "had in 1847 outlined the kinetical theory of gases in his 'Mathematical Physics'" but names no chapter or page; the theory is spread over these three places, and all three were chosen with pjdhiro. Volume 1 has no transcription and no Internet Archive scan; the text was read from the page images of the Harvard copy on Google Books (id=nH0tAAAAYAAJ), and the formulas were checked by calculation. The experimental works Herapath cites were not checked. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a person.

#### ウィリアム・ジェームズの「I と Me」を、原典で読む
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/william-james-self-ja.html

A reading guide to William James's writings on the self and consciousness, all public domain: Psychology: Briefer Course (London: Macmillan, 1892), ch.12 "The Self"; The Principles of Psychology (New York: Holt, 1890), ch.10 "The Consciousness of Self" and ch.9 "The Stream of Thought"; The Varieties of Religious Experience (Longmans, 1902); and "Does 'Consciousness' Exist?" (Journal of Philosophy, Psychology and Scientific Methods 1, 1904, pp.477–491). A table gives the reading order, where to open each work (Internet Archive page links and the Classics in the History of Psychology full texts), and what is there. Each section then gives key sentences, the English original first and a Japanese translation below, with page numbers: James divides the total self into the I (the self as knower) and the Me (the self as known) as "discriminated aspects" and not separate things; the Me includes all that a man can call his; a thought distinguishes what belongs to its own Ego by its warmth and intimacy; the sense of personal identity rests on resemblance and continuity; each Thought is born an owner and dies owned; the passing Thought itself is the only verifiable thinker; consciousness flows like a stream with a fringe; mystical states are ineffable, noetic, transient and passive; and consciousness names a function, knowing, not an entity. The sentences were chosen by Claude and their pages checked against the scans; errors in the York texts ("if flows", "I breath", "the knowing", "one if its") were corrected from the scans. Later research (Gallagher & Zahavi, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Guillot 2017) and George Herbert Mead's "I" and "me" (Mind, Self, and Society, 1934, §22) are given as links and summaries only. Not to be confused with the page on Henry James Sr.'s Substance and Shadow. The translation is by Claude (AI) and has not been reviewed by a human.

#### ジェームズに辿り着くまで
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/to-james.html

A diary-like independent page recording one "aha" moment of pjdhiro, subtitled "the warm feeling of I, and a dry breathing sound". He had taken the difference between the English I and me as grammar. Then, in object-oriented programming, he re-noticed the sense of pointing at something as "that"; in shikan meditation, what he had taken as I separated into me; and one morning, half awake, he heard a dry breathing sound and thinks that the me was absent. From this he noticed that he lives as a composite of I and me. Each chapter is a card of his words, a short answer by Claude, and one passage from William James checked against the scans, read only after the experience: the Me and the I as "discriminated aspects" (Briefer Course 1892, p.176), the Me as all one can call "me" (Principles 1890, p.291), the me as an aggregate of things known and the I as not an aggregate (pp.400–401), the present moment as "the darkest" (p.341), "warmth and intimacy" (pp.331, 333), and "the 'I breathe' which actually does accompany them" (1904, p.491). Fold-outs add Zhiyi's Mohe Zhiguan and the Linji lu on looking back at the one who observes, Guillot (2017) on for-me-ness, me-ness and mineness, and Mead's "I" and "me". In pjdhiro's felt sense the warmth comes from I alone and the me side felt dry. He proposes the axis of the witness for telling I from me: the seeing side is I, and everything that can be pointed at, thoughts and the thought "I" included, is me; he places the sameness of the self in that witness, which stays the same even while dreaming, whereas James places the felt sameness in the warmth and continuity of the me (pp.334–335, 337). Read on this axis, warmth that can be pointed at sits on the me side and warmth attached to seeing itself on the I side; this mapping is Claude's reading. In the breathing chapter, pjdhiro likens the morning experience to a ghost that only witnesses and has no body; he has never experienced depersonalization himself and drew the likeness from other people's accounts he had read. Translations are by Claude.

#### 聞こえていなかった呼吸の音
URL: https://uminomae.github.io/project-design-theory/reader/breath-filter.html

An independent page, subtitled "the correction before signals rise to consciousness, and me". It starts from pjdhiro's experience of hearing his own breathing as a dry sound on waking, with no "me" (the self as known) present, and his provisional conclusion that "the correction of hearing had stopped". It then looks at where one's own breathing sound is normally turned down. In the ear, the normally closed Eustachian tube keeps the energy of one's own voice and breathing away from the middle ear; with a patulous Eustachian tube one hears one's own breathing (Bance, Tysome & Smith 2019; Kawamura et al. 2019; bone-conducted body sounds in superior canal dehiscence, Ward, Carey & Minor 2017). In the brain, the sensory results of one's own movements are anticipated and attenuated (self-tickling, Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith 1998; self-triggered sounds, Martikainen, Kaneko & Hari 2005; one's own speech, Ventura, Nagarajan & Houde 2009; corollary discharge, Crapse & Sommer 2008; precision, Brown et al. 2013). What reaches consciousness is the hypothesis that best explains the signals (Hohwy 2012), breathing is normally automatic (Herrero et al. 2018), and much bodily feeling is prediction (Barrett & Simmons 2015; Seth 2013). James wrote that "the nucleus of the 'me' is always the bodily existence felt to be present at the time" (1890, p.400). Seth, Suzuki & Critchley (2012) proposed a model of the sense of presence and of chronic depersonalization; the page notes that it is not applied to a single morning experience, and quotes pjdhiro's own words that he has never experienced depersonalization. The last section puts forward, as a hypothesis, that one stopped correction in the brain (not the Eustachian tube) may account for hearing the breath, and, as Claude's reading, also for the absence of me.

## Using This Repository for a Love-Driven Development Review

To review a paper or text using the view of "Love駆動開発と呼びたいもの β" as the yardstick, use an LLM that can fetch the repository (e.g. Claude Code, Codex) and follow the README section 「Love駆動開発の視点でレビューに使うとき」: https://github.com/uminomae/project-design-theory#love駆動開発の視点でレビューに使うとき
- Fetch (or read the raw URLs below without cloning): `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/uminomae/project-design-theory`
- Must read (about 70-80k tokens): the full `docs/rules/stance.md` (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/uminomae/project-design-theory/main/docs/rules/stance.md, pjdhiro's view and way of judging) and `docs/rules/corrections.md` (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/uminomae/project-design-theory/main/docs/rules/corrections.md, misreadings LLMs tend to repeat), and the overview of the reader page. If the window allows: the full source `pd/knowledge/research/love-driven-dev/READER-love-driven-dev.md` (about 200k tokens). Open the rest only when the README's signposts say a topic needs it. The repository as a whole is far larger than any context window.
- The conditions and nuances of the view (what each statement answered, which readings were rejected) are in those rule files, not in the public pages. This file and the public pages alone are not enough for such a review.
- Love-Driven Development is pjdhiro's theory from naive personal experience, offered as a hypothesis. A review written this way is the LLM's reading, not pjdhiro's judgment.
